title: Look into node weighting
body: We're currently weighting the nodes by their volume elements, so the error should be the total force balance error in the domain. But it seems like this fluctuates a lot as you vary the number of nodes and basis functions (I would assume that for a given guess the total error shouldn't depend strongly on the discretization).

title: (R0, Z0, r, lambda) independent variables instead of (R, Z)
body: We are currently using R & Z as the independent variables. This might be an inefficient discretization in spectral space because we are restricted to using the SFL coordinates. Alternatively, we could use R0, Z0, r, lambda with: This has two potential advantages: 1. More efficient spectral representation (fewer Fourier modes required). 2. The BC can be applied as a linear constraint (satisfied exactly at each iteration). But it also has the potential disadvantage that the flux surfaces will be highly sensitive to the magnetic axis position (R0, Z0). We should add this alternative discretization as an option to test if it is ever superior to the existing approach.

body:
Major updates:
- Fixed the issues with building docs on RTD
- scalar objective now minimzied log(1+f^2) rather than just f^2. While mathematically equivalent, the gradients are now better behaved (effectively normalized by the local function value) which seems to improve convergence a bit. - Added script for automating search for good continuation settings
- Added class for computing jacobian on multiple GPUs (or a single gpu/cpu but using way less memory)

- Updated a bunch of stuff to support latest version of JAX

- stellarator symmetric node pattern now works with both direct and fft methods for zernike transform

Minor updates:
- added some pretty printing and colors for error messages etc to make them clearer to see
- cleaned up the way timing is done, so there is one timer object with multiple clocks running
- timing output should also be more human readable, and is returned by the continuation function for later analysis
- cleaned up documentation a bit

title: Get symmetric nodes and fft method to work together
body:
Right now using symmetric nodes requires using the direct method for the zernike transform, which is a lot slower. 

With fft, no symmetry:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/22567458/97833208-df34ef00-1ca2-11eb-8551-3ce84ef49335.png)
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/22567458/97833218-e8be5700-1ca2-11eb-83fd-408093cb7069.png)

With symmetry & direct method:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/22567458/97833244-fa076380-1ca2-11eb-96d2-eb32c7205bb5.png)
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/22567458/97833261-01c70800-1ca3-11eb-9e54-7e6a7c125719.png)

All these tests were using the w7x case with m,n = 12, mnodes,nnodes=18

Using symmetry and the direct method gives slightly better compile time for the gradient, but is waay slower for pretty much everything else, both compiling and evaluating. 
As it is now, using symmetry really isn't worth it, despite it reducing the dimension of the system by a half.

We could probably switch to using a different set of "symmetric" nodes that arent technically the right symmetry nodes but would work with the fft. Since we're already oversampling it's probably ok to not use the exact right nodes.
We could alternatively figure out how to redo the fft to work with an arbitrary node pattern (though from some earlier testing, doing the fourier and zernike transforms in the opposite order slows the transform part down,though it might be worth it)

Another thing to note is that the direct method uses a TON more memory when JIT compiling the first time (I kept running out even with 32 gigs) so thats another reason to use the fft, especially for high res

title: Cache computed values of Configuration for plotting/analysis
body:
When making plots we end up needing to calculate the same underlying quantities several times, so it would be efficient to compute them once and cache them.

See https://docs.python.org/3/library/functools.html#functools.lru_cache
or https://pypi.org/project/cached-property/

We'd need to break up some of the functions into smaller chunks to make things more efficient.

Note that we likely _don't_ want to cache the actual compute functions that get called by the optimizer, so we might want to have separate wrapper functions that do the caching.

IE:
`def fun(x):`
`    do something

`@lru_cache`
`def fun_cached(x):`
`    return fun(x)`

title: Use seperate "load' method instead of keyword in standard init
body:
Right now all the IOable classes have a keyword arg in init "load_from", which is used to instantiate from a saved file.
However, this means that all of the other args need to have default values, even ones which should be mandatory, so its a bit confusing.
Ideally we would have a regular init method, where mandatory args must always be specified, and others have some default value.
We'd then have a separate method for loading from a saved file

eg:

class foo():
    
    def __init__(self, arg1, arg2, arg3="default"):
        self.arg1 = arg1
        self.arg2 = arg2
        self.arg3 = arg3
        
    @classmethod
    def load(cls, load_from):
        # create a blank object bypassing init
        self = cls.__new__(cls)
        
        # open the file and set attribute like:
        # for attr in file:
        #     setattr(self, attr)
        
        # to set other secondary stuff that wasnt saved possibly:
        self._after_init()

        return self

It would also be good to have an easy way of combining different objectives with a given weight, so that we could do something like

title: Better syntax for continuation parameter arrays
body:
In the input files, specifying the continuation parameter arrays can be kind of a pain, especially as you go to high resolution and possibly lots of small perturbation steps. It might be good to add some additional syntactic sugar to make things easier.
A few ideas:
`4:2:12` would be expanded in the matlab style to `4,6,8,10,12`, allowing easy specification of equal steps
`12x4` would be expanded as `12,12,12,12`, allowing easy repetition of the same value for multiple steps
`16...` would be treated as "use 16 for the rest of the iterations", so you could do something like `4,8,16....` and combine that with some other array that was 20 long without having to write out 16 a bunch of times.

title: Equilibrium solutions disagree with documentation
body:
### Configuration/Environment

Currently Loaded Modulefiles:

1. gmp-6.2.0
2. mpfr-4.1.0

Using device: CPU, with 113.99 GB available memory

### Steps to reproduce the issue

Following the "Using DESC interactively" section of the documentation exactly, I tried to reproduce the same plot for "eq1". As per the steps in the given example, first, an equilibrium was obtained with elliptical boundary surface and zero pressure. Then it was perturbed to include a quadratic pressure profile. This script includes all the commands I gave:
[perturb_example1.txt](https://github.com/ddudt/DESC/files/6558432/perturb_example1.txt)
The flux surfaces I get are different than what is given in the documentation:
![flux_sf_eq1](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/84903460/119939624-c5ffd280-bf53-11eb-9e7e-c94ef0f7362d.png)

To confirm whether this was a valid equilibrium solution, I plotted the force balance error:
![eq1_Ferror](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/84903460/119939777-f8a9cb00-bf53-11eb-84e1-13659e78ab48.png)

It seems that perturbing the vacuum solution did not yield an equilibrium solution. However, I am not sure if a low error should be expected after perturbation.
I tried to solve this perturbed equilibrium 'eq1' using `eq1.solve(verbose=2, ftol=1e-4);`. A low error is obtained, but the flux surfaces are not the same as those in the documentation:
![eq1solved_Ferror](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/84903460/119940289-9604ff00-bf54-11eb-87f5-c2ccb13bd249.png) ![eq1solved_fluxsf](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/84903460/119940536-f431e200-bf54-11eb-815d-6c1a8a821234.png)

Next, I tested the high beta D-shaped tokamak example given in the cited paper. This also did not give the same equilibrium solution. I started with a vacuum solution and perturbed the pressure profile as per the profile given in the paper.
Here is my script:
[high_beta_D.txt](https://github.com/ddudt/DESC/files/6559092/high_beta_D.txt)

The perturbed flux surfaces are different that the ones in the paper. The force balance error for the perturbed equilibrium is, once again, too large:
![eq1_flux_sf](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/84903460/119945679-66a5c080-bf5b-11eb-84ac-2bcb44a57019.png) ![eq1_Ferror](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/84903460/119945810-8f2dba80-bf5b-11eb-9d13-dd0aa56fc220.png)

I also tried to solve for the perturbed equilibrium explicitly with `eq1.solve(verbose=2, ftol=1e-4);`,. The resulting flux surfaces do not match the ones in the paper (although the force balance error is low):
![eq1solved_flux_sf](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/84903460/119946267-0fecb680-bf5c-11eb-954b-14cb2b312cec.png) ![eq1solved_Ferror](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/84903460/119946676-7ffb3c80-bf5c-11eb-9e53-07945b1c3cdb.png)


I solved the same equilibrium using the command line interface and the input file provided in the repository (I changed only the maximum pressure to match the paper). I used `python3.9 -m desc -o output.out -pp -v ../DESC/examples/DESC/DSHAPE`. The input file, the flux surface plot and the force balance error plot are attached. These do not match the paper either:
[DSHAPE.txt](https://github.com/ddudt/DESC/files/6559158/DSHAPE.txt)
![flux_sf](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/84903460/119948256-44fa0880-bf5e-11eb-9ad5-8945b656ca63.png) ![Ferror](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/84903460/119948270-47f4f900-bf5e-11eb-99fb-4708e3632225.png)


Note: Since the solution in the paper matches the VMEC solution but the one obtained with the current DESC version does not, I thought it best to report this issue. Perhaps it is because of the recent modifications to the code since the example in documentation seems to be using "DESC version 0.3.22+40.g14b6afa.dirty". If so, and the developers are aware of it, I apologize for the inconvenience.

title: IO Updates
body:
Bug fixes:
- Fix bug in pickle IO that prevented objects with jitted attributes from being saved, pickling now only saves essential information.

Changes:
- Added generic `load` function for loading objects without knowing what class they are
- Removed usage of "==" operator between DESC objects in favor of
`obj1.eq(obj2)`. Equivalence is defined as "if saved and loaded, the two objects would
be the same," so it ignores equality in trivially recomputeable attributes
and focuses on the actual physics of the objects being compared.
- Concentric grids are now up-down symmetric when symmetry is not enforced

Backend:
- Remove `_object_lib_` from io, instead, now use built in dynamic importing
to import the correct classes at runtime
-Avoids needing to import classes in lots of files just so they can be in the `_object_lib_`,
makes adding new stuff a lot easier.
-Changed `name` in io stuff to `__class__` to avoid conflicts with actual `name` attributes

Resolves #81

title: Differentiable basis function evaluation
body:
Right now we manually compute derivatives of the basis functions and use them in transform objects, but in some cases it may be better to be able to differentiate the basis functions themselves with autodiff, I'm thinking mainly when the evaluation points are changing constantly so precomputing and using a transform is wasteful and also non-differentiable (eg, when finding inverse coordinates, tracing fieldlines, etc)

For the fourier stuff this should be as simple as replacing ``np`` with ``jnp``, and possibly rewriting the functions to use ``jnp.vectorize`` instead of manual vectorization
For the zernike/jacobi stuff the main issue is numerical stability since the direct evaluation can be problematic for large l,m.
Possible solutions: 
- find a good recurrence relation that can also compute analytic derivatives
- use definition of zernike in terms of jacobi : https://mathworld.wolfram.com/ZernikePolynomial.html 
  - and the jacobi derivative: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobi_polynomials#Derivatives
- Define new jax primitive for zernike evaluation (kind of a pain)

title: Zernike evaluation
body:
- This PR addresses two major things: speed, and differentiability:
- Previously, obtaining accurate zernike evaluation required using
extended precision arithmetic that meant we couldnt' use JAX for
that part of the calculation, making it both slow when the grid changes
on each iteration (as with computing inverse coordinate mappings and
field line tracing etc), and also non differentiable.
- A new method has been implemented that uses identities for the zernike
polynomials in terms of jacobi polynomials, and a stable iterative
evaluation for the jacobi polynomials and binomial coefficients.
- Accuracy seems on par or better than the old method using extended
precision, at least for a given amount of computation time.
- There is some overhead from JIT compilation, but seems to pay off well
for high resolution
- Also implemented a new "unique" option for basis.evaluate to first
reduce the work by finding unique combos of nodes/modes. Previously
this was done inside each basis function evaluation, but doing it on the
outside should be more efficient and makes the underlying functions
differentiable.
- Also refactored fourier series evaluation. 
- Rather than using nested conditionals and recursive functions,
switched to just shifting the argument to account for
derivatives and odd/even parity. Seems quite a bit faster, especially
when using jit Rather than using nested conditionals and recursive functions,
switched to just shifting the argument to account for
derivatives and odd/even parity. Seems quite a bit faster, especially
when using jit
- Transforms used in the profile class weren't built by default,
causing them to be built when first called which is under jit,
meaning they would be recomputed every time instead of caching
the transform as expected. Updated to now build transforms by default.

Resolves #117

title: Timing Benchmarks
body:
Over the past few months our test suite has gotten a lot slower. In many ways this is expected, as we add more tests to comprehensively test more of the code, but it also makes it harder to tell when changes are actually slowing the code down. It would be good to start including systematic timing benchmarks as part of our regular test suite.

Pytest has a plugin to do something like that: https://pytest-benchmark.readthedocs.io/en/latest/index.html
And there's a Github Action to do it as part of our regular CI stuff and even make a spiffy webpage with the results: https://github.com/rhysd/github-action-benchmark

I don't think it would be too hard to set up, we could start with benchmarking the basic equilibrium solves for the DSHAPE and SOLOVEV solutions, plus hopefully a simple stellarator case. We could also include micro benchmarks for smaller parts of the code like computing transforms, compiling jacobians, etc.

On a related note, we should also try to reduce the overall testing time where possible (using lower resolution, smaller arrays, etc), we're coming up on 20-30 mins depending on hardware.

title: Objectives
body:
This pull request introduces the new objective function API outlined in #78 

Significant changes:
- The "compute functions" in `compute_funs.py` are reorganized to only take the arguments each function requires. Functions build on each other, and parameters are added to request the order of derivatives needed. All outputs are stored in a single dictionary of terms. 
- The `Equilibrium` class no longer "owns" an optimizer or objective, and does not build its own transforms. 
- The `ObjectiveFunction` class is a "super-objective" that combines multiple "sub-objectives" which follow the ABC `_Objective` class. 
- Each sub-objective function can be used as either an "objective" (minimized during optimization) or a "constraint" (enforced exactly). 
- Each sub-objective function takes unique inputs that can be specified by a grid/surface/etc. or use default values from an `Equilibrium`. 
- Each sub-objective is responsible for building its own transforms or other constant matrices, and is also responsible for computing its own derivatives. 
- The super-objective dynamically builds the state vector with the independent variables from each sub-objective, and also combines the function values and derivatives by combining the outputs from each sub-objective. 
- The super-objective only takes a single argument (the state vector x or y). Perturbations are now performed wrt the full state vector y, which contains all of the individual parameters. 

Continued work:
- The compute functions could be further optimized to reduce redundant calculations. 
- This new objective structure allows computations for each sub-objective to be performed in parallel, but this is not yet implemented. 
- Only linear objective functions can be used as constraints; using nonlinear constraints may be desirable in the future. 
- More methods could be added to make the user interface more friendly when working with the objective functions for custom applications. 

Resolves #78

Due to ``jit``'d attributes/methods not being pickleable, all ``IOAble`` objects override the default pickling method to only save the relevant data. However, the `copy.deepcopy` operation also uses pickle under the hood, so some data (ie, things not in ``_io_attrs_``) would not be copied properly. When computing basic benchmark cases (dshape, heliotron), the force error is slightly worse on objectives branch than master, and the comparisons to vmec fail. The main change is the grid rotation, but using the old rotation actually gives even worse errors.
One possible cause is the projection of the full state vector ``y`` into the optimization vector ``x``. Because we include lots more in the state now, this projection is different, and may be taking a different slice through the optimization landscape.

We should test more to figure out if this is the case, and if so find a way to recover the old behavior, possibly by:
- weighting least norm solution for projection (see #139)
- Computing null space independently for each constraint, then combining them rather than combining then finding nullspace (to avoid issues with massive difference in scale)

title: Slower compilation / perturbations on objectives branch
body:
For several benchmark cases, the perturbations take longer on the objectives branch, likely because we are perturbing wrt more things. Also, because we use Jy in the perturbations, and Jx in the optimization, we have to compile twice, whereas before they both used Jx so the compilation only happened once.

Possible solutions:
- Use Jx in perturbations
- Use jvp to get Jc rather than projecting Jy

title: Initialization
body:
Adds new ways to set the initial flux surfaces for an equilibrium:
- Supplying an interior surface, by setting ``surface.rho``. The surface will be scaled inwards and outwards accordingly, so that the equilibrium has that surface at the specified value of rho.
- Specifying R,Z (and optionally lambda) at a grid of nodes in rho, theta, zeta. Could be useful for interfacing with other equilibrium codes with different bases etc, and for interfacing with near-axis expansion codes.

- Also unifies the API for ``surface.change_resolution``, so that a triple of L,M,N can be passed, or just the two that are relevant for the given surface.
- Adds method ``equilibrium.get_surface_at`` which returns a ``FourierRZToroidalSurface`` or ``ZernikeRZToroidalSection`` representing the plasma at a specified rho or zeta coordinate.

Resolves #166

title: Fix bug when changing resolution in continuation
body:
- Changing only grid or only spectral resolution would lead to objectives getting copied and re-used instead of recreated, so the old compiled function with the wrong resolution was used, causing a shape error. 
- Seems to have been caused by transform objects living in both objectives and equilibria, so updating one also changed the other
- Making local copies of transforms in objectives seems to fix it for now.
- Kind of a kludge, but new objectives function API should eliminate this entirely by making transforms only properties of objectives.

title: Easily wrap user defined objective functions
body:
In addition to the predefined objectives, we should be able to wrap a function from the user in an ``Objective`` to make it easy to work with the rest of the code. One possibility would be to allow the user to define any function of the form ``func(data) -> ndarray`` where ``data`` is a dictionary containing any of the quantities from ``data_index``. We can then parse the user supplied function to find out what data is actually needed and create an objective that first calls the necessary compute function to get the raw variables, then calls the user function to calculate the final desired quantity.

The following snippet shows an example of parsing user code to determine which variables are needed:
```
def foo(data):
    x = data["x"]
    y = data["y"]
    z = x*y
    return z

import inspect, re
pattern = r"data\[(.*?)\]"
src = inspect.getsource(foo)
variables = re.findall(pattern, src)
variables = [s.replace("'", "").replace('"', "") for s in variables]
print(variables)
>>> ['x', 'y']
```

title: Having multiple constraints that target the same argument is not supported currently
body:
On objectives branch, If you have more than one constraint that has the same argument (i.e. two constraints that both take in `R_lmn`), then when the constraint `Ainv` matrices are being built inside of `_build_linear_constraints`, whichever constraint comes later in the constraints list will overwrite the `Ainv` matrix of the other constraint (since both are being accessed by the same dict key)

This came up when I was running with two constraints that both targeted `L_lmn`, the lambda axis constraint and the Poincare constraint that constrained lambda at the zeta=0 plane. Can be seen in this code block:

```
from desc.objectives import ObjectiveFunction
from desc.objectives import (
    LCFSBoundaryR,
    LCFSBoundaryZ,
    LambdaGauge,
    PoincareLambda,
    FixedPressure,
    FixedIota,
    FixedPsi,
    PoincareBoundaryR,
    PoincareBoundaryZ,
)
from desc.objectives import ForceBalance
from desc.basis import ZernikePolynomial, FourierZernikeBasis,FourierZernike_to_PoincareZernikePolynomial
from desc.geometry import ZernikeRZToroidalSection
from desc.equilibrium import EquilibriaFamily, Equilibrium


eq = EquilibriaFamily.load(load_from='../examples/DESC/SOLOVEV_output.h5')[-1]

Rb_lmn, Rb_basis = FourierZernike_to_PoincareZernikePolynomial(eq.R_lmn, eq.R_basis)
Zb_lmn, Zb_basis = FourierZernike_to_PoincareZernikePolynomial(eq.Z_lmn, eq.Z_basis)

surf = ZernikeRZToroidalSection(
    R_lmn=Rb_lmn,
    modes_R=Rb_basis.modes[:, :2].astype(int),
    Z_lmn=Zb_lmn,
    modes_Z=Zb_basis.modes[:, :2].astype(int),
    spectral_indexing=eq._spectral_indexing,
)

eq_poin = Equilibrium(
    surface=surf,
    pressure=eq.pressure,
    iota=eq.iota,
    Psi=eq.Psi,  # flux (in Webers) within the last closed flux surface
    NFP=eq.NFP,  # number of field periods
    L=eq.L,  # radial spectral resolution
    M=eq.M,  # poloidal spectral resolution
    N=eq.N,  # toroidal spectral resolution
    L_grid=eq.L_grid,  # real space radial resolution, slightly oversampled
    M_grid=eq.M_grid,  # real space poloidal resolution, slightly oversampled
    N_grid=eq.N_grid,  # real space toroidal resolution
    sym=True,  # explicitly enforce stellarator symmetry
    bdry_mode="poincare",
)
eq_poin.L_lmn = (
    eq.L_lmn
)  # initialize the poincare eq with the lambda of the original eq
eq_poin.change_resolution(
    eq_poin.L, eq_poin.M, 1
)  # add toroidal modes to the equilibrium
eq_poin.N_grid = 2  # set resolution of toroidal grid

constraints = (
    PoincareBoundaryR(),
    PoincareBoundaryZ(),
    PoincareLambda(),  # this constrains lambda at the zeta=0 surface, using the eq's current value of lambda
    LambdaGauge(),
    FixedPressure(),
    FixedIota(),
    FixedPsi(),
)
objectives = ForceBalance()
obj = ObjectiveFunction(objectives, constraints)
obj.build(eq_poin)
obj.rebuild_constraints(eq_poin) # fails because the LambdaGauge Ainv is being used for the PoincareLambda, so the size is incorrect as they have different targets
```

title: Jacobian sign fixes
body:
Ensures DESC always works in a coordinate system with positive coordinate jacobian.

The sign of the jacobian is determined by the orientation of theta. If theta increases clockwise, it is right handed (positive jacobian), otherwise it is left handed (negative jacobian)

When the jacobian is negative, (ie left handed coordinates) some of our equations are incorrect and some of the output vector quantities (B,J,etc) are off by a sign.

To ensure consistency, we now convert any inputs to have a right handed system (ie, theta increasing clockwise). This is summarized below:

- sign( $B_\phi$ ) determined by $\Psi$
- $\Psi$ * $\iota$ > 0 = $B_{poloidal}$ goes clockwise = $J_\phi$ > 0


| $\Psi$ | $\iota$ | $B_{\phi}$ | $B_{poloidal}$ | $J_\phi$ |
|---|---|---|-----|---|
| - | - | - | CW  | + |
| - | + | - | CCW | - |
| + | - | + | CCW | - |
| + | + | + | CW  | + |



TODO:

- [x] fix signs in outputs saved in `desc.examples`
- [x] fix signs in inputs in `examples/DESC`
- [x] double check vmec output
- [x] regenerate precise QH test benchmarks with correct jacobian

title: Inaccurate concentric grid due to round-off at high N_grid values
body:
I noticed that if I use N_grid = 30, the grid module runs into an error at line 710, which reads:
`z = np.arange(0, 2 * np.pi / NFP, dz)`
The trace reads:
`Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "descrun.py", line 6, in <module>
    eq1.change_resolution(N_grid=30)
  File "/srv/home/sapatil/.conda/envs/descenv/lib/python3.10/site-packages/desc/equilibrium.py", line 319, in change_resolution
    self._set_grid()
  File "/srv/home/sapatil/.conda/envs/descenv/lib/python3.10/site-packages/desc/equilibrium.py", line 176, in _set_grid
    self._grid = ConcentricGrid(
  File "/srv/home/sapatil/.conda/envs/descenv/lib/python3.10/site-packages/desc/grid.py", line 559, in __init__
    self._nodes, self._weights = self._create_nodes(
  File "/srv/home/sapatil/.conda/envs/descenv/lib/python3.10/site-packages/desc/grid.py", line 672, in _create_nodes
    nodes = np.stack([r, t, z]).T
  File "<__array_function__ internals>", line 5, in stack
  File "/srv/home/sapatil/.local/lib/python3.10/site-packages/numpy/core/shape_base.py", line 426, in stack
    raise ValueError('all input arrays must have the same shape')
ValueError: all input arrays must have the same shape`

I found that this is a result of round-off error in `dz` from line 709:
`dz = 2 * np.pi / (NFP * (2 * N + 1))`
One solution is to use np.linspace at line 710:
`z = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi / NFP, 2 * N + 2)[:-1]`
I have attached a section of the source code (v 0.4.9) that creates the grid. This can be used as an independent script. The issue can be reproduced when N=30 or higher.
This was a minor bug, but I thought it may be worth reporting.
[conc_grid.txt](https://github.com/PlasmaControl/DESC/files/8951477/conc_grid.txt)

title: Hotfix
body:
Change `LinearGrid` API to be more consistent with other `Grid` classes: 
- L, M, N now correspond to the grid spectral resolution, rather than the number of grid points
- rho, theta, zeta can be passed as integers to specify the number of grid points (functionality that used to belong to L, M, N)
- rho, theta, zeta still retain their functionality of specifying coordinate values if they are not integers
- Other code that depends on `LinearGrid` was updated accordingly to use the new syntax

Poloidal grid points are now shifted when `sym=True` to give correct averages over a flux surface.

title: Add Jacobian Sign Change as test of unestedness
body:
Currently we check for nested surfaces during the equilibrium solve with the `is_nested` method of equilibrium which checks the geometry of a given number of flux surfaces. However a faster way would be to just check that the sign of the jacobian is only one value (if there is a sign change, that means jacobian is zero somewhere and thus we have unnested surfaces.

title: VMEC to DESC input file conversion for toroidal current constrained cases
body:
[By default](https://github.com/jonathanschilling/educational_VMEC/blob/0999e1e66d0ba8407e587084787cbf0d92c8dab2/src/profile_functions.f#L305), VMEC `AC` coefficients constrain the radial derivative of the net enclosed toroidal current. So, when converting a VMEC to DESC input file, we need to also check for `pcurr_type` and [change the conversion accordingly](https://github.com/hiddenSymmetries/VMEC2000/blob/e5de70486235be997e95ca4a129441d51b796226/Sources/Input_Output/readin.f#L128), integrating in `s` if it is the default `power_series` or if `pcurr_type` is not specified at all

also need to ensure we read in the `CURTOR` parameter, which is an overall scale factor (in Amps) on the enclosed net toroidal current profile (so by default NOT a scale factor on the `AC` coefficients directly, as those describe `I'(s)`). [See here](https://github.com/jonathanschilling/educational_VMEC/blob/7ce6c6093a3adf06c8cb37681b6ea81549632c87/src/profil1d.f90#L81) for multiplication, where `currv = mu0*curtor` as [seen here](https://github.com/jonathanschilling/educational_VMEC/blob/fbdebe2a4324573f5763b6a2c1ad8d8d8a20ca2c/src/readin.f90#L84)

The new method is quite a bit slower (so defaults to the old method), but seems to use less memory (smaller intermediate jacobians) and will also allow us to parallelize using MPI in the future.

title: More efficient compute functions
body:
Right now we use the ``check_derivs`` function to determine what things to compute within a given compute function. As we add more things, this can get slower and slower because we compute extra things that may not be needed and forward mode autodiff will still keep track of them. I've been thinking about a new method, outlined below.

The main idea is that each compute function would only compute a single quantity from the data index. Most of them could be simple one liner lambda functions.
Each would take 3 args: 
``data`` : a dictionary of real space things computed up to this point
``coeffs``: dictionary of spectral coefficients
``transforms``: dictionary of transform and profile objects
(maybe also something for kwargs etc)

The data index would be updated to include a list of what things that quantity directly depends on, like so:
```
data_index["lambda_z"] = {
    "label": "\\partial_{\\zeta} \\lambda",
    "units": "rad",
    "units_long": "radians",
    "description": "Poloidal stream function, first toroidal derivative",
    "fun": lambda data, coeffs, transforms: transforms['L'].transform(coeffs['L_lmn'], dz=1),
    "depends_on": []
    "dim": 1,
    "L_derivs": [[0, 0, 1]],
}
data_index["B^theta"] = {
    "label": "B^{\\theta}",
    "units": "T \\cdot m^{-1}",
    "units_long": "Tesla / meters",
    "description": "Contravariant poloidal component of magnetic field",
    "fun": lambda data, coeffs, transforms: data["B0"] * (data["iota"] - data["lambda_z"])
    "depends_on" : ["B0", "iota", "lambda_z"],
    "dim": 1,
    "R_derivs": [[0, 0, 0], [1, 0, 0], [0, 1, 0], [0, 0, 1]],
    "L_derivs": [[0, 0, 0], [0, 1, 0], [0, 0, 1]],
}
```

Note that ``lambda_z`` doesn't depend on anything, since its directly computed from the spectral coefficients. The L_derivs etc still work the same to figure out what orders of derivatives are needed (could possibly rework it so the list of derivs is also created recursively)

All this would be wrapped by one main compute funciton like so:

```
def compute(qty, data, coeffs, transforms):
	if qty in data:
		return data
	for thing in data_index[qty]['depends_on']:
		if thing not in data:
                        # compute dependencies recursively
			data = compute(thing, data, coeffs, transforms)
	data[qty] = data_index[qty]["fun"](data, coeffs, transforms)
	return data
```

This would eliminate the possibility of computing more things than needed, and ideally make adding new computeable things a lot easier.

- [x] #331
- [x] #332
- [x] #356
- [x] #357

title: LinearGrids with same nodes have different spacing/weights
body:
There are 2 methods for creating a grid with a specified number of nodes (as opposed to specified basis resolution). The first (which isn't officially documented) is to just pass integers for `theta`, `zeta` etc, which will linearly space that many nodes, as in `grid1` below. The other is to pass in arrays directly, as is done with `grid2` below.
```
ntheta = 5
nzeta = 4
NFP = 3
grid1 = LinearGrid(rho=1, theta=ntheta, zeta=nzeta, NFP=NFP, endpoint=False)
grid2 = LinearGrid(rho=1, theta=np.linspace(0,2*np.pi,ntheta, endpoint=False), zeta=np.linspace(0,2*np.pi/NFP, nzeta, endpoint=False), NFP=NFP)

print("Nodes agree:", np.allclose(grid1.nodes, grid2.nodes))
print("Spacing agree:", np.allclose(grid1.spacing, grid2.spacing))
```
Gives that the nodes agree but spacing doesn't. 

The spacing for `grid1` seems correct, as it has all nodes having the same spacing and weights. While the spacing for `grid2` seems way off, with `dz` ranging from 0.2 to 4.9

This further causes the weights to be computed incorrectly, possibly giving the wrong averages etc.

title: Solving vacuum equilibria from input file is somewhat broken
body:
If an input file has `objective = vacuum` and no profiles given, the equilibrium is generated with a current profile. However, this is not constrained during optimization, and the resulting equilibrium can have a current profile with very large coefficients (~1e5). These seem to cancel to give a reasonable (if oscillatory) current profile, but it could cause issues with the optimizer since the step length its taking are O(1e4). 

Explicitly including `i = 0` in the input file seems to work, allowing iota to vary and giving reasonable step sizes. 

We should probably define what sort of behavior we want when `objective = vacuum`. Does this mean:
- Minimize J with I=0
- Minimize J with iota free
- something else?

title: Weights are scaled incorrectly on grids with duplicate nodes
body:
_Originally posted in https://github.com/PlasmaControl/DESC/pull/279#discussion_r987394648_
Link to comment with notebook to test https://github.com/PlasmaControl/DESC/pull/279#issuecomment-1263193774

Our `_scale_weights` does not reduce duplicate node weight correctly

A simple example of this is `nrho=1, ntheta=5, nzeta=1, endpoint=True`. The correct theta spacing for this `[0.78539816 1.57079633 1.57079633 1.57079633 0.78539816]` with drho = 1 always, dzeta = 2pi always. And at this point in the code that is what the spacing is.

`_scale_weights` then detects the duplicate nodes at 0 and 2pi and scales down the node volume drho * dtheta * dzeta. So the end result of the grid spacing is:
```
[[0.82982653 0.65174424 5.21395388]
 [1.04551592 1.64229256 6.56917025]
 [1.04551592 1.64229256 6.56917025]
 [1.04551592 1.64229256 6.56917025]
 [0.82982653 0.65174424 5.21395388]]
```
The reason I think this is wrong is because a rho surface integral uses the dtheta * dzeta portion of the node volume, ignoring drho. Similar for other surface labels. If we wanted the correct rho surface integral we should leave the drho unchanged and scale up /down dtheta * dzeta.

title: Optimizer
body:
- Cleans up and removes a lot of old/unused/unecessary code
- Gets rid of custom Hessian update stuff in favor of just using scipy's BFGS class
- Adds new options for setting the initial trust region in `lsqtr` and `fmintr` via the option `initial_trust_radius`:
  - A numeric value uses that value.
  - `"scipy"` uses the default from scipy, which is the norm of the scaled `x`. This was also the default value in prior versions of DESC and will remain so for the time being.
  - `"conngould"` uses a recommended value from Conn & Gould that scales the trust region so that the Cauchy step is on the boundary - generally more conservative than `"scipy"`
  - `"mix"` uses a geometric mean between `"scipy"` and `"conngould"`
- Adds a basic stochastic gradient descent optimizer `sgd` for noisy objectives. Currently only supports either a fixed step size or standard momentum. In the future may be updated to include other step size rules such as RMSProp or Adam.
- Adds utility function for performing modified Cholesky factorizations of indefinite matrices, needed to ensure that the `dogleg` and `subspace` methods work for general Hessian matrices.

Logging overhaul2
body:
Primary addition is in __init__.py; adds functions set_console_logging and set_logfile_logging.  All print statements have been routed to python's logging module, which requires libraries to not log anything natively- will need to use these two functions to view logging information in console or written to file.

To write to logs, instead of print statments, one uses "logging.warning("string"), where 'warning can be replaced by the log level of your choice.  Activating a lower log level will display all statments at that level or higher.  A quick call to one of the "set logging" functions in a fresh new environment will need to be gotten used to.  The lowercase is important!  Do not use "logging.WARNING("string").  This just returns the numeric value of the log level.

The native log levels - listed as follows- allow numeric inputs as well- levels "DEBUG", "INFO", "WARNING", "ERROR", "CRITICAL" correspond to 10, 20, 30, 40, and 50 respectively.

Currently, I have written most standard log messages as "WARNING", termination and error messages as "ERROR", with "CRITICAL" being unused, and synonymous with silent running.  "INFO" displays info on individual iterations, and "DEBUG" shows timing info along with all inner and outer loop iteration info.

Added a flag for logging levels, and made the --verbose and --quiet flags refer to set_console_logging() levels.  Also added --logging, which can be used as -l, -ll, and -lll as well to access WARNING, INFO, and DEBUG respectively.

Other changes- currently some of scipy's functions we use automatically write to stdout through print statements- which is annoying, and required helper functions to capture their writing to stdout and redirect it to the base logging system.  Which is exactly the reason libraries are not supposed to have authoritative printing and logging behaviours; our compliance with the logging library is agnostic to user intent.

Old tests for the functionality of our i/o have been rewritten, but might probably require more tests now to make sure these function as intended- especially as the way I've written the scipy stdout capturing function requires python3.

Questions: 
1.  Currently set_console_logging admits a parameter to print to stderr, or stdout- if we don't plan to use this, should remove it.  Same with set_logfile_logging, admiting file names other than desc.log.
2. Logfile default is set to DEBUG to show all possible info, console logging is set to WARNING to display less info.  Should this change?
3.  We have some error and warning messages using print statements, and not the standard library's warning and error modules we sometimes import.  I have converted these to logging.error() statements- should I reroute those to the standard error modules?  Or should I rewrite all error and warning info to be handled by the logger?
4.  Currently logging mostly matches our prior 0, 1, 2 levels of verbosity.  The higher level ERROR could be made more use of- and CRITICAL is currently not used at all.  Do we want to change what the different log levels mean currently? 
5.  Currently I have the logfile desc.log being overwritten any time the log level is set to a different value, with a flag to make this optional.  Do we want overwriting old log files to be the default, or not-overwriting old desc.log log files to be the default?
6.  If we're swapping from print statements everywhere to python's core logging, what's the best way to alert users to new functionality, given DESC no longer emits messages aside from initialization messages by default?

body:
Right now we compute everything in physical units (Amps, Newtons, Tesla etc). This is good for physics comparison, but makes weighting between different objectives in multi-objective optimization a bit trickier.

In the past we've tried non-dimensionalizing things dynamically by defining a dimensionless metric, but if the normalization is allowed to change during optimization it can cause issues (not to mention making the problem more nonlinear).

Instead we should pre-compute some static scaling factors based on "characteristic scales" in the problem (ie, toroidal flux + area gives a characteristic B field, pressure + radius gives a characteristic force, etc). The goal isn't to be exact, but just to get things all to roughly the same order of magnitude so they can be compared more meaningfully, similar to how we usually plot force error normalized by a pressure gradient.

I couldn't add `"elongation"` to the `data_index` because it requires two separate grids: a quadrature grid to compute the surface areas, and a linear grid on the boundary surface to compute the perimeters. We could use the same LinearGrid for both computations, but that would be sub-optimal for the area calculations. So all of the new logic is only in the objective function itself. I'm open to suggestions for improvement.

title: Constraints have wrong derivatives when building at initialization
body:
Any `Objective` can be passed an `Equilibrium` when initialized to build the objective, or otherwise it can be built later.  The former method gives incorrect derivative values.  This has only been tested with linear objectives that are typically used for constraints (specifically, the problem seems to only be with `FixBoundaryR` and `FixBoundaryZ`).  

Minimal working example to reproduce the bug:
```
import numpy as np
from desc.equilibrium import Equilibrium
from desc.objectives import FixBoundaryR, FixBoundaryZ

eq = Equilibrium(M=3, N=1)

# initialize the constraints without building
constraints_1 = (
    FixBoundaryR(fixed_boundary=False),
    FixBoundaryZ(fixed_boundary=False),
    FixBoundaryR(fixed_boundary=True),
    FixBoundaryZ(fixed_boundary=True),
)
print("method 1: without building\n")
for obj in constraints_1:
    obj.build(eq)
    arg = obj.args[0]
    A = obj.derivatives["jac"][arg](np.zeros(obj.dimensions[arg]))
    print("constraint {}: A.shape = {}, max(|A|) = {}".format(
        obj.name, A.shape, np.max(np.abs(A))))

# build the constraints while initializing
constraints_2 = (
    FixBoundaryR(fixed_boundary=False, eq=eq),
    FixBoundaryZ(fixed_boundary=False, eq=eq),
    FixBoundaryR(fixed_boundary=True, eq=eq),
    FixBoundaryZ(fixed_boundary=True, eq=eq),
)
print("\nmethod 2: with building\n")
for obj in constraints_2:
    arg = obj.args[0]
    A = obj.derivatives["jac"][arg](np.zeros(obj.dimensions[arg]))
    print("constraint {}: A.shape = {}, max(|A|) = {}".format(
        obj.name, A.shape, np.max(np.abs(A))))
```
And the output: 
```
method 1: without building

constraint lcfs R: A.shape = (21, 21), max(|A|) = 1.0
constraint lcfs Z: A.shape = (21, 21), max(|A|) = 1.0
constraint lcfs R: A.shape = (21, 30), max(|A|) = 1.0
constraint lcfs Z: A.shape = (21, 30), max(|A|) = 1.0

method 2: with building

constraint lcfs R: A.shape = (21, 21), max(|A|) = 0.0
constraint lcfs Z: A.shape = (21, 21), max(|A|) = 0.0
constraint lcfs R: A.shape = (21, 21), max(|A|) = 0.0
constraint lcfs Z: A.shape = (21, 21), max(|A|) = 0.0
```
"method 1" is correct.  "method 2" gives derivative matrices that are all zeros, and they are the wrong shape for `fixed_boundary=True`.

body:
MWE:

```

grid = LinearGrid(
    M=eq.M, N=eq.N, NFP=eq.NFP, rho=np.array([0.6, 0.8, 1.0]), sym=True
)

objective = ObjectiveFunction(
    (
        QuasisymmetryTwoTerm(weight=1e-2, helicity=(1, -eq.NFP), grid=grid),
        AspectRatio(target=8, weight=1e2),
    ),
    verbose=0,
)
R_modes = np.vstack(
    (
        [0, 0, 0],
        eq.surface.R_basis.modes[
            np.max(np.abs(eq.surface.R_basis.modes), 1) > n + 1, :
        ],
    )
)
Z_modes = eq.surface.Z_basis.modes[
    np.max(np.abs(eq.surface.Z_basis.modes), 1) > n + 1, :
]
constraints = (
    FixBoundaryR(modes=R_modes, fixed_boundary=True, normalize=False),
    FixBoundaryZ(modes=Z_modes, fixed_boundary=True, normalize=False),
)
for con in constraints:
    con.build(eq, verbose=0)
objective.build(eq)
from desc.objectives.utils import factorize_linear_constraints
xp, A, Ainv, b, Z, unfixed_idx, project, recover = factorize_linear_constraints(
    constraints,
    objective.args,
)

from scipy.linalg import block_diag
from desc.compute import arg_order
A_full = block_diag(*[A[arg] for arg in arg_order if arg in A.keys()])
b_full = jnp.concatenate([b[arg] for arg in arg_order if arg in b.keys()])

x1 = objective.x(eq)
x2 = recover(project(x1))
print(np.max(np.abs(x1-x2)))
print(np.max(np.abs(A_full @ xp - b_full)))
print(np.max(np.abs(A_full @ x1 - b_full)))
print(np.max(np.abs(A_full @ x2 - b_full)))
print(np.max(np.abs(A_full @ Z)))
```

Gives the following output:
```

1.0

so doing project + recover gives a different answer, and the initial x from `objective.x` doesn't satisfy the constraints?

title: Ensure transforms build correctly even with empty grid
Simplify |B| derivative computations
body:
The formulas for the partial derivates of $|B|$ were derived from the equation:
$B = \sqrt{\left(B^\theta\right)^2 e_\theta \cdot e_\theta + \left(B^\zeta\right)^2 e_\zeta \cdot e_\zeta + 2 B^\theta B^\zeta e_\theta \cdot e_\zeta}$
These formulas could likely be simplified by instead using the equivalent definition: 
$B = \sqrt{B^\theta B_\theta + B^\zeta B_\zeta}$

This would greatly reduce the number of lines of code used by these functions, and could also provide some slight performance improvements for the quasi-symmetry computations.

title: Duplicate node spacing
body:
Resolves #286 for the common case of a duplicate node at theta = 2pi and zeta = 2pi / NFP (endpoint).

For grids with an arbitrary number/position of duplicate nodes, it is tricky to weight the spacing correctly for rho, theta, and zeta surfaces simultaneously. I was a bit stubborn and had a mostly working implementation of this, but I don't think it's worth it over the more practical solution of deleting duplicate nodes prior to grid construction.

title: Remaining bugs with duplicate nodes, add grid developer guide
body:
- [x] Squash bugs
    A list of bug fixes follows. The use case that would uncover these bugs is rather narrow, which is why it wasn't detected by previous tests, and is unlikely to affect most stuff. All of these bugs involve duplicate nodes, however, none of them were introduced by #386 . This PR just finds bugs that were missed by that one.

    - Fixed issue where theta and zeta surface integrals on grids with duplicate node at 0 and 2 pi (or 2 pi/NFP) (e.g. when endpoint=True) computed a value that was off by a factor of 2 only on the surface at 0 and 2 pi. All other surfaces were computed correctly.
    In other words, 2 elements of the returned array of length `grid.num_surface_label` were off by factor 2.
    - More massaging of inputs so that the grid class works with weird inputs. This is required for correctness of some of the algorithms, but unlikely to be the cause of any bugs as a runtime error would have been raised immediately.
    - Added logic so `LinearGrid`s with duplicate nodes and `symmetry` have correct weights and spacing.
    - If the user supplies an incorrect marker for endpoint, for example by providing `endpoint=False` to the `LinearGrid` constructor while also providing arrays with nodes that include a duplicate endpoint, the weights would be computed incorrectly. This was fixed so that the correct weights are computed  regardless of the user's tricks.

- [x] Add bug catchers
    - many more tests
- [x] Add bug repellent
    - add walk-through of `grid.py` to developer guide explaining everything with nice visuals

title: Bootstrap current
body:
This PR introduces two main components. The first is a compute function for the bootstrap current, `"<J*B> Redl"`, using the formula by Redl et al, Physics of Plasmas 28, 022502 (2021). This formula for the bootstrap current is valid in axisymmetry, quasi-axisymmetry, and quasi-helical symmetry, but not in other stellarators. The bootstrap calculation uses the new kinetic profiles (electron density, electron temperature, ion temperature, and atomic number) of `Equilibrium` objects. The 2nd new component is an `Objective`, presently named `BootstrapRedlConsistency`, for optimizing the current or iota profile to be consistent with the Redl formula. The objective is essentially the same expression used in Landreman Buller Drevlak, Physics of Plasmas 29, 082501 (2022).

For examples of using the new objective, see the last two tests in `tests/test_bootstrap.py`. The basic idea is to include `BootstrapRedlConsistency(helicity=(1,0))` or `BootstrapRedlConsistency(helicity=(1,NFP))` in your objective, while removing constraints on iota or current. When optimizing prescribed-iota equilibria, you should exclude `FixIota()` from the constraints. When optimizing a prescribed-current equilibrium, you should typically still include `FixCurrent(indices=[0])` in the constraints, so the current is mostly allowed to vary, but it still goes to 0 on axis as it should. When optimizing prescribed-current equilibria, it seems important to set `gtol=0` in the optimizer to prevent it from terminating early, I think because the current parameters in SI units are >> 1.

For some of the tests, in which the bootstrap current is compared to full drift-kinetic calculations with the SFINCS code, DESC input and output files for the relevant configurations were added to `tests/inputs`. Hope this is ok.

As this is my first significant PR, just let me know if there's anything I should pay attention to. For instance I wasn't sure what to pay attention to in the output of `pylint` and `flake8`.

title: Improve handling of indefinite hessian matrices in fmintr
body:
The trust region subproblems used in `fmintr` require the Hessian matrix to be positive definite. In the case that it isn't, we perform a modified Cholesky factorization such that the factors give a positive definite approximation to the true Hessian. The previous method for doing this modified factorization, while robust, is quite slow, likely because it's not taking advantage of optimized low level BLAS stuff.

This PR updates the modified Cholesky routine to use a bisection search to find a small diagonal correction to ensure the factors are positive definite. This is much faster in practice, often only 2-3x more expensive that a regular un-modified Cholesky factorization, and the results seem to be about as good on most problems I've tested with.

Some benchmarking for matrix of size 8000x8000:
```
Old cholmod
2min 3s ± 2.15 s per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1 loop each)
New cholmod
6.25 s ± 119 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1 loop each)
Regular cholesky
1.83 s ± 67.8 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1 loop each)

Previously, if the user requests data from `eq.compute` on a specified grid, that grid is also used to compute any volume or surface averages, leading to incorrect results in many cases.

This PR adds a pre-computation to `eq.compute` that checks if any of the quantities requested (or their dependencies) are volume or surface averages, and first performs those calculations on a full grid to ensure the correct result. title: Logging overhaul3
body:
Adds DESC-specific logger that is automatically set up to write to a logfile and output to console as a normal print statement would, adds some helper functions for adding other logging handlers to DESC logger.  It also generates a file called "desc.log".

Logging can now happen at several levels, and loggers will display all logs of a given level and higher.  These are DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, and CRITICAL.

Currently we use DEBUG for inner-loop timing and iteration information, and INFO for most standard logs.  Warnings from the 'warnings' module will automatically be logged as WARNING level logs, though raising errors will not automatically generate ERROR logs.

To use logger, you will need the following lines before you invoke it:
`import logging`
`logger = logging.getLogger("DESC_logger")`

Writing a log statement can be done by replacing a print statement with an invocation to the logger, and / or one of its log levels:
`logger.debug("Lowest level message")`
`logger.info("Standard DESC info level message")`
`logger.warning("Message that will log with the same severity as a 'warnings.warn()' statement")`
`logger.error("High level message")`
`logger.critical("Highest level log message)`

To allow a function to change the verbosity level of the DESC logger, you will want initiate the DESC logger as usual with
`import logging`
`logger = logging.getLogger("DESC_logger")`

Then in your function, include the following logic:
`if verbose == 0:`
`    logger = set_console_logging(console_log_level="CRITICAL")`
`if verbose == 1:`
`    logger = set_console_logging(console_log_level="INFO")`
`if verbose == 2:`
`    logger = set_console_logging(console_log_level="DEBUG")`

This removes the need for constant verbosity checks; the logger knows what message level the user has set verbosity to, so you can use 'logger.debug("Msg") and 'logger.info("Msg") calls whenever and the output will sort itself out.

Currently a logfile log has the following format:
`2023-02-28 16:56:31.603 :: DESC_logger :: INFO ::  File: objective_funs  Func: build  Line: 189  ::  Building objective: force `

A console log has the following format- but is probably too long, and should be changed before merging- it could be we want no formatting, so it will display like a normal print statement but still be logged.
`INFO     DESC_logger:equilibrium.py:523 Start of solver`

Log levels will display in a color-coded fashion in the console.  Once we know exactly how much information we want to display where, I can finish the unit tests for the newly added functions.

This has changed how tests that compared stdout to expected output strings work, so now a logger is made to capture output to compare to the desired string.  If we decide not to format console logs at all, the old method can be reinstated.

title: Add missing attributes to new classes
elongation toroidal surface angle
body:
Elongation `"a_major/a_minor"` is computed at toroidal cross-sections, and the `Elongation` objective function penalizes the maximum elongation of all the toroidal angles. 

The vector normal to the cross-section used to compute the elongation must be parallel to the magnetic axis. These cross-section "cuts" are not at a constant toroidal angle $\phi$ if the magnetic axis is non-planar. However, the present code does compute the elongation at cross-sections of constant toroidal angle $\phi$. 

Finding the toroidal angles that give a cross-section normal to the magnetic axis would involve solving a sub-problem. The correction may be small for most equilibria, but can be significant for those with a very non-planar axis.

title: How to handle NAE O(rho) stellarator symmetry, but O(rho^2) asymmetric solutions with NAE constraints
body:
When the NAE equilibrium is stellarator asymmetric bc of O(r^2) effects, the DESC equilibrium fit is also asymmetric. BUT, the NAE O(r) constraints are stellarator symmetric. 

This leads to the first problem, which is that the constraints will be setting the stellarator asymmetric parts of the equilibrium's O(r) coefficients to roughly 0, which can cause some weirdness when solving

To allevaite the issue I thought to drop any NAE constraints whose target was below a threshold value (of like 1e-12 or so). However, this means when solving, the equilibrium's stellarator asymmetric coefficients are free to move as they wish, and this results in a completely different looking equilibrium than the NAE equilibrium (as expected I guess, since there is so much more freedom that we are not constraining).

title: Automatically select step sizes for continuation method

title: Objective.compute_scalar independent of grid resolution
body:
This PR attempts to resolve most of the problems raised in Issue #482. Most importantly, it makes sure that all objectives with "local" errors now have their `compute_scalar` values roughly independent of the grid resolution, both when normalized and not. 

These changes also have `Objective.normalization` now only used to make the values dimensionless; it removes the need to reference `Objective.dim_f` in the compute logic. 

Also updates `Objective.print_value` to print the min/max/mean of the error instead of just the total, and uses abs error when target is 0, and only prints total error for linear objectives (assumed they're used as exactly satisfied constraints so we don't need lots of details). A

Printing should also be more intuitive, printing the actual value of the aspect ratio, volume etc rather than the error.

Resolves #482

title: Add interfaces for constrained optimizers
body:
- Adds interfaces to `trust-constr` and `SLSQP` methods of `scipy.optimize.minimize`. These methods can handle general nonlinear constraints, though their performance on badly scaled problems like those encountered in stellarator optimi isn't great.
- `Objective` and `ObjectiveFunction` `compute` methods have now been separated into `compute_unscaled` which returns the raw physics value of the objective, `compute_scaled`, which returns the normalized value, and `compute_scaled_error` which returns the normalized difference between the physics value and the target/bounds. Similarly, `jac_scaled` and `jac_unscaled` are the relevant derivatives (note that `jac_scaled` is equivalent to `jac_scaled_error` as the constant target drops out). `grad` and `hess` methods still correspond to `compute_scalar` which returns the sum of squares of `compute_scaled_error`
- Adds new `ObjectiveFunction` attributes `target_scaled` and `bounds_scaled` which return vectors of the scaled values from each sub-objective.
- Adds automatic scaling of variables for `scipy.optimize.minimize` methods, using the hessian at the initial point.
- Ensures objectives don't have both bounds and target set at the same time. This occasionally caused issues if one of them had a default value without the user realizing.
- Adds a bunch of missing docstrings and args to linear objectives- Adds documentation on how to interface with new optimizers.
- Adds a documentation notebook with a simple example of using constrained optimizers
- Adds a table of optimizer info to docs

Resolves #418

title: Add iota calclulation from field line integration of a coilset/magnetic field
body:
When doing field line integration from a magnetic field, would be useful to also get out the iota values. Multiple ways to do this but the easiest to implement initially is probbaly to just do the literal definition for iota,

$$ \iota = \lim_{n\rightarrow \infty} \frac{1}{n} \sum_1^n \Delta \theta_n$$

where $\Delta \theta_n$ is the change in poloidal angle in the $\phi=0$ plane from the $n-1$ toroidal transit to the $n$ th toroidal transit, which could be calculated as $arctan(\frac{Z-Z_{axis}}{R-R_{axis}})$


Where iota is calculated in FOCUS, as an example

https://github.com/PrincetonUniversity/FOCUS/blob/be28c104bebc1b4ea281547b03fc1e9fab34e8e2/sources/poinplot.f90#L113

title: Dp/softmin
body:
Implement softmin as an option for PlasmaVesselDistance objective
- Uses jax.scipy.special.logsumexp for the softmax implementation, and softmin is just `-(softmax(-array))`
- adds a parameter `alpha` that determines how approximate the `softmin` is, with `softmin -> min` as `alpha -> inf`
- softmin will also automatically multiply by an effective alpha to make the values of an array at least > 1 (to try to help avoid inaccuracies that occur when values <1 are used with the softmin which results in inaccurate estimates or even incorrect signs)

softmax is defined as $log(e^x + e^y)$ 
The parameter alpha can be added to this to make it more closely approximate the true max $$max(x,y) \approx lim_{\alpha\rightarrow \infty} log(e^{\alpha x} + e^{\alpha y}) / \alpha$$

Then softmin is defined as `-softmax(-array)`

title: Dp/XYZ_coils_and_BNORM
body:
The main thing this PR adds is a new curve/coil class (SplineXYZ), I/O support for MAKEGRID-formatted coils, and the ability to read in and save BNORM-style files containing information on B normal on plasma surface.

also has pytest ignore RuntimeWarnings from Cython about numpy array sizes changing, as if they are just a warning then they are benign, and if it would ever cause issues it would probably instead be a RuntimeError (https://stackoverflow.com/questions/40845304/runtimewarning-numpy-dtype-size-changed-may-indicate-binary-incompatibility)

resolves #460

## SplineXYZCurve and SplineXYZCoil
- New classes which accept coordinates in real space cartesian, and spline fits them with an arbitrary angle (which by default is normalized arclength). This is the coil format typically used in MAKEGRID-formatted coils files outputted by other codes like REGCOIL and FOCUS, and is the format accepted by MAKEGRID. 
- type of spline is any of the types that exist in `desc/interpolate.py`

## Coil and MAKEGRID Conventions
Where possible the conventions have been chosen to be similar to what is already used and expected by the [MAKEGRID code](https://princetonuniversity.github.io/STELLOPT/MAKEGRID.html). This was chosen to make DESC able to read in MAKEGRID coilis files from other sources, and to be able to have DESC-saved files be readable by other codes as well.

 - CoilSets have an NFP attribute, but this is only for informational purposes of what the nominal magnetic field periodicity is for this CoilSet. It does not affect any computations
 - Therefore, CoilSet objects should always have the full CoilSet in them, even if there is a discrete rotational symmetry.
 - CoilGroups (that is, the groups of coils which can be assigned the same current in MAKEGRID) must be handled by the user by specifying the name of each coil in the CoilSet when saving to the MAKEGRID formatted file. This could be changed in the future to also have a CoilSet name be used to provide the coil group, but as of right now this is the current support for that compatibility

title: eq.solved = False when max iterations reached
body:
If `eq.solve` terminates because it reaches the maximum iteration limit, then the Equilibrium gets assigned the attribute `eq.solved = False`. However, it could still be a good equilibrium solution in this case. This can be problematic when saving the equilibrium as a wout file for use with external codes, since the wout property is assigned as `ier_flag = not eq.solved`. It should be noted that even when the optimization terminates "successfully" and assigns `eq.solved = True`, this does not guarantee that the solution is in fact a good equilibrium. 

Potential solutions:

1. Remove the `Equilibrium.solved` attribute and always output `ier_flag = False` in the wout files. This puts more burden on the user to check that they have a good solution, but avoids input/output errors with other codes. 
2. Change the `Equilibrium.solved` property to always check the volume averaged normalized force balance error against some threshold. This would always return the desired result, at the cost of requiring an extra computation every time it is called.

title: Start making users build before optimizing
body:
We had discussed this in the context of having multiple different optimizeable objects that we need to keep track of. The idea was to require the user to call `objective.build` themselves with the correct objects, rather than always calling it with `eq`. 

A better option might be to simply require the user to pass in the correct optimizeable objects at objective init, but delay the expensive building part until `.build` is actually called, but this time `.build` would not take any arguments.

IE:

```python
# binds the objective and the optimized object, 
# but doesn't actually do the expensive build part yet
objective1 = ForceBalance(eq=eq)
objective2 = QuadraticFlux(eq=eq, coilset=coilset)

# throws an error, needs eq
objective3 = AspectRatio(target=5)

objective1.build()
objective2.build()
```

That way things would be correctly bound together, but avoids the user having to manually call `build` a bunch of times (and in principle, we could call `build` automatically, without the user ever having to).

title: Utility for rescaling equilibria to given major radius and field strength
body:
It's common in publications to compare equilibria after re-scaling them to the same major radius and field strength. It would be nice to have a utility to do this automatically.

I think it's fairly straightforward. If we define 2 scale factors:

$c_R = R_{0, desired} / R_{0}$

$c_B = B_{desired} / B$

then we should just have to multiply `R_lmn` and `Z_lmn` by $c_R$, and multiply `Psi` by $c_B c_R^2$.

$J \times B \sim \Psi^2$ so to preserve force balance and beta, we'd also need to multiply $\nabla p$ by $c_B^2c_R^4$, which works out to multiplying `pressure` by $c_B^2c_R^5$ (the extra factor of $c_R$ is due to the $\nabla$ operator, which goes like $1/R$). For temperature and density its trickier since they can vary independently but a simple one would just be to multiply both by the square root.

For fixed current we'd also need to multiply `current` by $c_R c_B$ (I think, based on $I = \int B \cdot dl$)

One possible solution is to allow each objective to have a "loss" or "reduction" applied to the raw output. Any jax transformable function that takes in and returns a single array should be ok.

title: Ensure derivatives of basis are zero for unused coordinates
body:
Currently taking derivatives of a basis wrt coordinates not in the basis basically ignores the derivative argument and returns the wrong value.

eg
```
d/dr FourierSeries(z) == FourierSeries(z)
d/dz PowerSeries(r) == PowerSeries(r)
etc
```

Which seems wrong, and could cause some issues.

This PR fixes this by always returning 0 if taking a derivative wrt to an ignored coordinate.

title: Add `data_index` aliases for mixed partial derivatives etc.
body:
There are a lot of things in the `data_index` that are effectively symmetric under a permutation of the coordinates, for example, the metric tensor, partial derivatives etc.

eg: `R_rt == R_tr`, `g^zt == g^tz` etc.

Right now we only have one permutation of each (usually the alphabetically first one, eg `X_rt` instead of `X_tr`) in the `data_index`.

It would be convenient if we also somehow had aliases or something so that you can call `compute` with either and get the same answer.

For example, if I want all the metric tensor elements and their derivatives, I could do:

```python
for i in ["r", "t", "z"]:
    for j in ["r", "t", "z"]:
        coeffs = eq.compute("g^" + i + j, grid=grid, data=coeffs)
        for d in ["r", "t", "z"]:
            coeffs = eq.compute("g^" + i + j + "_" + d, grid=grid, data=coeffs)
```

Right now this fails because half of the things don't exist in the `data_index`

title: Turn DESC classes into JAX pytrees
body:
In JAX parlance, a "pytree" is a (possibly nested) container of arrays and data, like `list`, `dict`, `tuple` etc. Basically, it means its a type that JAX knows about, and can be passed into jit compiled functions as normal, without having to close over or declare as a static argument.

see: https://jax.readthedocs.io/en/latest/pytrees.html

It would be useful, and possibly necessary, to allow DESC classes to act as pytrees. I *think* it should be straightforward:

- need to define a function/method for each class that converts the class data into a tuple of arrays or other jax types
- another function to re-create the object from a tuple

We can probably reuse a lot of the io infrastructure, with the caveat that we don't save all attributes of objects but we probably do want to use all of them in the pytree, so maybe a bit complicated.

title: Make desc classes compatible with jax pytrees
body:
- When we "close over" stuff like transforms and other big arrays in the `objective.compute` methods, it can lead to larger than expected memory usage and longer compile times as those matrices get baked into the computational graph that JAX compiles.
- Previously, we couldn't pass these things in as extra arguments, because arguments to jit compiled funcitons must be jax types (ndarray, or pytree)
- This PR registers all desc `IOAble` classes as jax pytrees allowing them to cross the jit boundary unaltered. 
- The base `IOAble` class has a default method for converting things to pytrees which treats `int`, `bool`, `str` and a few other types as constants, since those are usually used as indices/flags etc that shouldn't be changed during optimization. If a particular class needs other behavior, you can override the default method (but the default seems to work fine for basically all of our existing classes).
- Also adds a new attribute to all objectives, `objective.constants` which is a dictionary of constant properties, such as transforms and profiles. This is then passed into `objective.compute` as an extra arg/kwarg depending on the situation.
- Combined with #539 this significantly reduces memory usage, such that we can go up to `L=M=N=20` with the grid oversampled by 2 in each direction on a single A100 gpu. Free boundary can go up to at least `L=M=N=12` (haven't tried higher but probably can).


Resolves #532 
Resolves #540

title: Add retry step to codecov upload
Add "looped" option for computing jacobian matrix
body:
The standard way jax computes the jacobian matrix is with ``vmap(jvp(fun))``, which attempts to vectorize the jacobian vector product to compute the entire jacobian at once. This is usually the fastest way, but because it has to materialize all the intermediate matrices in memory at the same time, it limits the resolution we can use.

Another option is to instead manually loop over the columns of the jacobian and build it one at a time. This is a bit slower, but much more memory efficient.

Some profiling results:

[looped](https://gist.github.com/f0uriest/9f5f915bede37d3f68868b29979e8bd2)
[master](https://gist.github.com/f0uriest/c3d7c15642bae9e563048c4beb0b9787)

On master, on an A100, we max out around L=M=N=14, with the nodes oversampled by 2 in each direction (probably overkill)

With the looped jacobian for the same specs, we max out around L=M=N=20.

Overall speed is a bit slower with the looped jacobian: 
![image](https://github.com/PlasmaControl/DESC/assets/22567458/1c9f83ad-fcce-4d3c-82e0-1d3fd3d201f2)

But still a very useful option when we need higher resolution.

title: flip sign of current when Jacobian is negative
body:
In `ensure_positive_jacobian` we flip the sign of the rotational transform profile if the original Jacobian is negative. This should happen whether the equilibrium is using an iota profile or a current profile, but the existing code did not handle the case of a current profile. This PR also flips the sign of the current profile in these cases. 

A test is added to ensure that loading a VMEC equilibrium with either `profile="iota"` or `profile="current"` gives equilibria with the same profiles. (This discrepancy was the issue that prompted this fix.)

title: Change default lagrange multipliers in augmented lagrangian
body:
We previously defaulted to using the "least squares" estimates for the multipliers which works well if you start near the solution, but if you're far from the solution its a bad estimate. If the multipliers are way off it can send the whole thing off in some weird direction, and may never converge.

This changes the default initial guess for the multipliers to be 0 which makes the initial step a basic penalty method which should always converge. The old behavior can be recovered by passing ``options={"initial_multipliers": "least_squares"}``

title: plot_qs_error bug fix
body:
The default parameters for `plot_qs_error` are:
- `M_booz = 2 * eq.M`
- compute grid resolution of `eq.M_grid`

Typically `eq.M_grid` defaults to `2 * eq.M`, and in this case the Boozer spectrum is being computed on a grid with the same number of nodes as modes (no over-sampling). This can result in the plotted `f_B` errors looking much worse than they truly are. 

This PR increases the default compute grid resolution by a factor of two so the Boozer spectrum in the typical case is computed more accurately.

title: Chebyshev polynomials
body:
Adds Basis functions and classes for shifted Chebyshev polynomials. 
- `ChebyshevPolynomial` can be used for radial Profiles. 
- `ChebyshevDoubleFourierSeries` is used for the omnigenity mapping parameters. 

The Chebyshev polynomials are computed from the trigonometric definition $T_n(x) = \cos(n \arccos(x))$ where $x = 2\rho-1$. This makes the evaluations fast for JIT compilation, but is messy to differentiate. Derivatives of the polynomials are not implemented yet, since they are not needed for the omnigenity calculations. To add this functionality in the future, it may be better to compute the Chebyshev polynomials through the recurrence relations.

title: Implement vector-jacobian products for objectives

Currently we evaluate this directly using the full Jacobian matrix, but this is a bit wasteful since it can be evaluated much faster with reverse mode AD. JAX already has functionality for this exact sort of thing, so we'd just need to wrap that and add an interface like `objective.jvp`

title: Magnetic axis limits and new variables
body:
[Math to compute the rotational transform in DESC.pdf](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/16120690/rotational_transform_and_limit.pdf)


- [x]  Resolves #486
